## Objectives

+ How statistics is used in the business world.
+ About the sources of data and the methods for collecting it.
+ How to classify data by the measurement approach.
+ To distinguish between time series and cross-sectional data.
+ To distinguish between descriptive, inferential and predictive statistics.
+ About the ethical implications of misusing statistics.
+ Organize a reproducible, AI-assisted analysis.
+ Use **Claude** and **Python** to retrieve economic data from the Federal
  Reserve Economic Data (**FRED**) service.
+ Verify the identity, units, frequency, date range, and missing values of
  downloaded data.
+ Record the provenance of every data set you analyze.

## Our AI-assisted analytics workflow

This semester we will use **Claude** as an analytical collaborator. Claude can
help us write, run, explain, and debug computer code, and it can execute that
code and show us the result. It can often complete calculations much faster
than we can complete them manually. However, speed does not guarantee that the
data, method, or interpretation is appropriate.

Our work will follow this sequence:

1. **Define the business question.** What decision or claim will the analysis
   support?
2. **Specify the data.** What does each observation represent? Which
   variables, dates, units, and populations are relevant?
3. **Direct Claude.** Give Claude a precise task, relevant constraints, and a
   required output.
4. **Run reproducible code.** Preserve the code and record where the data came
   from.
5. **Verify the work.** Inspect the data, calculations, assumptions, and output
   instead of accepting them automatically.
6. **Interpret and communicate.** Translate results into a defensible business
   conclusion and disclose important limitations.

::: {.scarlet}
**Claude is a capable junior analyst, not the decision maker.** You are
responsible for the analytical specification, verification, interpretation, and
final recommendation.
:::

### The one rule that governs everything else

::: {.charcoal}
**Every number you report must come from code that was actually executed.**
Never take a figure from an assistant's prose. If you cannot point to the cell
that produced a number, the number does not go in your submission.
:::

An assistant that writes a paragraph containing plausible-looking values has
not performed an analysis. An assistant that runs a script and shows you its
output has. The difference is invisible in the writing and decisive in the
result.

### Organizing an analysis

You will do most of your work this semester in Claude's code-execution
environment: you upload a data file and a starting script, and Claude runs
Python on them and shows you the output. There is nothing to install.

Even in that setting, keep the same discipline a full project folder would
impose:

```text
Inputs      -- the data file exactly as it was downloaded, unmodified
Program     -- the script that transforms inputs into results
Outputs     -- tables and figures, always regenerated by running the program
Provenance  -- a written record of where the data came from
```

We do not silently overwrite or hand-edit source data. If a number needs to
change, the program changes, and we run it again. This is what makes an
analysis *reproducible*: someone else can start from your inputs and your
program and arrive at your outputs.

A provenance record is short and it is not optional:

```text
Series:      DFF - Federal Funds Effective Rate
Source:      Federal Reserve Economic Data (FRED), Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis
URL:         https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/DFF
Retrieved:   2026-08-24
Frequency:   Daily, 7-day
Units:       Percent, not seasonally adjusted
Date range:  2020-01-01 through 2026-08-21
Rows:        2,425
```

## Some uses of Data Analytics and models

### Marketing research

**Taste tests** have been a staple of marketing research. Kellogg researchers,
for example, would provide consumers with **Cheez-It** crackers and
**Nabisco's Cheese Nips**. The researchers would ask consumers to rate the
product. By repeating this research with thousands of consumers, the
researchers would establish trends in preferences across the market. This
research would shape product development. If you avoid the researchers armed
with clipboards in the mall (and everyone like you with similar tastes), your
preferences will not be reflected in the next evolution of snack food!

It is actually much more difficult to elude the market researchers today. Many
websites you visit are monitoring
[**clickthrough rates** (CTR)](https://support.google.com/google-ads/answer/2615875?hl=en).
We will say much more about **marketing research** in this class.

### Advertising

The television industry for decades has used
[**Nielsen Media Research**](https://markets.nielsen.com/us/en/about-us/panels/ratings-and-families/).
These ratings are based on data collected from a panel of US households. The
Nielsen researchers sample from these households to measure viewing habits and
preferences for the entire country. The design of these samples is critical in
ensuring that the results from the survey responses reflect the nation as a
whole. **Sampling strategies** and **statistical inferences** are a topic for
us this semester.

### Operations

**Quality control** is an important consideration for today's large scale
producers. As many production processes are **automated**, sampling from the
large quantities of goods produced in each period is a technique to assess
production quality. As no production process is perfect, quality control
engineers establish benchmarks for inherent variation in, say, product
dimensions. [**Six Sigma**](https://www.6sigma.us/six-sigma.php) is a
methodology intent on reducing this **inherent variation** to a small or
minuscule level. Our quality control engineers identify problems in the
production processes when they find production deformities outside the defined
benchmarks. Statistical **variation** is an important topic for our
investigations.

### Finance

Many economic events cannot be perfectly anticipated. This is particularly
troublesome given the experience of some economic shocks can have disruptive
change on a business. Moreover, many of these events cannot be avoided. For
example, if the global economy enters a recession, **pro cyclical** businesses
would more than likely experience sharp reductions in consumer demand.
Decisions regarding launching a new product line or new manufacturing facility
could have disastrous implications for a business if these launches coincided
with a recession. Finance professionals use **probability** as a tool to weight
potential outcomes across all potential business climate scenarios. As economic
conditions change, these probabilities are reassessed and the **average** or
**expected returns** from a business decision are recalculated. Modern
statistical spreadsheets and statistical packages are used to **cascade** the
changing probabilities across all upcoming or reversible decisions of the
business.

### Sports business

Insights regarding player performance that impacts team outcomes can be
exploited by a team if they can recognize undervalued traits in players.
Famously, the Oakland Athletics front office did exactly this by recognizing
that a statistical analysis identified players who were having large impacts on
positive team performance but were not being compensated for these
contributions (see [Moneyball](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moneyball_(film))).
This provided an opportunity for the organization to buy and **play** this
undervalued talent.

## Data

::: {.charcoal}
**Data** are values assigned to observations or measurements and are the
building blocks of statistical analysis.
:::

::: {.charcoal}
**Information** is data that are transformed into useful facts that can be used
for a specific purpose, such as making a decision.
:::

::: {.charcoal}
A **data set** is a collection of data points in a single application.
:::

::: {.charcoal}
**Structured data** are data that has been ordered into rows and columns (a
data table). The rows represent a distinct element (i.e., a client or a
person). The columns represent different characteristics that have been
measured for the distinct element (i.e., street address, postal code, vertical
jump).
:::

::: {.charcoal}
**Unstructured data** are data that is not ordered into data tables. Examples
include the characters in a tweet, the text from a news break, and the
transcript of a corporate report.
:::

::: {.charcoal}
**Secondary data** are data that somebody else has collected and made available
for others to use.
:::

::: {.charcoal}
**Primary data** are data that you have collected for your own use.
:::

::: {.charcoal}
**Direct observation** is a method of gathering data while the subjects of
interest are in their natural environment, often unaware that their behavior is
being recorded.
:::

::: {.charcoal}
A **focus group** is a direct observational technique whereby individuals are
often paid to discuss their attitudes toward products or services in a group
setting controlled by a moderator.
:::

::: {.charcoal}
An **experiment** is a method of gathering primary data by exposing subjects to
certain treatments and recording the data of interest.
:::

::: {.charcoal}
A **survey** is a method of collecting primary data by directly asking people a
series of questions. They can be administered by e-mail, via the web, through
snail mail, face to face, or over the telephone.
:::

### Two main types of data

::: {.charcoal}
**Quantitative data** use numerical values to measure a characteristic of
interest.
:::

::: {.charcoal}
**Qualitative data** use non-numerical values to assign labels to a
characteristic. For example, level-of-education may be the degree earned: Less
than High School, High School Diploma, Associates Degree, Bachelors Degree,
Masters Degree, Doctorate.
:::

### Classifying data by their measurement approach

::: {.charcoal}
**Nominal data** are data that are described as a category or a label. Examples
are marital status (married, single, divorced, widowed), or membership status
(yes, no).
:::

::: {.charcoal}
**Ordinal data** have all the properties of nominal data, with the added
feature that we can rank-order the values from highest to lowest.
:::

::: {.charcoal}
**Interval data** is strictly quantitative and allows us to measure the
differences between the categories with actual numbers in a meaningful way. For
example, temperatures, or product dimensions.
:::

::: {.charcoal}
**Ratio data** have all the features of interval data with the added benefit of
having a true zero point. *True zero*: If the phrase "twice as much" accurately
describes the relationship between two values that differ by a multiple of two,
the data can be considered *ratio data*.
:::

| Type     | Key Properties                                                                                     | Examples                                                                                                                                              | Notes                                                        |
|----------|----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|--------------------------------------------------------------|
| Nominal  | - Categories / labels only <br> - No order or ranking                                              | - Marital status: Married, Single, Divorced, Widowed <br> - Membership: Yes / No <br> - Hair color: Brown, Black, Blonde                               | Numbers (if used) are just codes, not meaningful values.     |
| Ordinal  | - Categories **with order** <br> - Differences between ranks not meaningful                        | - Education level: High School < College < Graduate < PhD <br> - Likert scale: Strongly Disagree → Strongly Agree <br> - Race positions: 1st, 2nd, 3rd | Can say "higher/lower," but can't quantify "how much higher." |
| Interval | - Numeric scale <br> - Differences are meaningful <br> - **No true zero** (ratios don't make sense) | - Temperature (°C, °F) <br> - Calendar years <br> - IQ scores <br> - Time of day (clock)                                                               | Can add/subtract, but "twice as much" is not valid.          |
| Ratio    | - All interval properties <br> - **True zero** (absence of what's measured) <br> - Ratios meaningful | - Age <br> - Weight <br> - Height <br> - Income <br> - Temperature in Kelvin                                                                           | Can multiply/divide: "twice as much" makes sense.            |

### Time series versus cross-sectional data

::: {.charcoal}
**Time series data** are values that correspond to specific measurements taken
over a range of time periods.
:::

The **Federal Funds Effective Rate** is the interest rate at which depository
institutions trade federal funds (balances held at Federal Reserve Banks) with
each other overnight. The FRED series identifier is **DFF**. Source:
[Federal Funds Effective Rate on FRED](https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/DFF).

## Claude Analytics Laboratory 1: Obtaining data from a data service

An **application programming interface (API)** is a documented way for one
computer program to request data or services from another. Instead of
downloading and editing a spreadsheet manually, we can write a reproducible
program that requests a defined FRED series. The program can be re-run tomorrow
and will pick up tomorrow's data; a spreadsheet you edited by hand cannot.

FRED exposes its data two ways, and the distinction matters for this course:

+ A **public CSV endpoint** that requires no credentials. It is an ordinary
  URL that returns ordinary CSV:

  ```text
  https://fred.stlouisfed.org/graph/fredgraph.csv?id=DFF&cosd=2020-01-01
  ```

  Paste that into a browser and you will get the data. This is what we will
  use for lecture work and Laboratory 1, because every student can run it
  immediately with nothing installed but `pandas`.

+ A **full REST API** at `api.stlouisfed.org` that requires a free personal
  API key and returns richer metadata. You will use this later in the Group
  Forecast Project. See the
  [FRED API documentation](https://fred.stlouisfed.org/docs/api/fred/series_observations.html).

The retrieval itself is done once, by your instructor, using a small course
module called `fred_tools.py` — it lives in
[`tools/`](https://github.com/jcrooker/mba775/tree/main/tools) in the course
repository if you want to read it. It converts FRED's `.` missing-value marker
to `NaN`, enforces the date and numeric types, and raises a clear error when a
series ID is wrong rather than returning a confusing half-parsed table.

You will not run it. Your exercises read the CSV it produced, which is
committed to the repository along with a record of exactly where each series
came from. That is deliberate: an analysis that depends on a live network
connection fails in ways that have nothing to do with the analysis.

::: {.charcoal}
When you do move to the keyed API, an API key is a **credential**. Never paste
a key into a prompt, a notebook, a rendered report, or anything you submit. If
a key is ever exposed, revoke it and request a new one.
:::

### If Claude says it cannot reach GitHub

You will see a reply along these lines:

> I don't have direct network access in this environment, and searching for
> the repository didn't surface it. If you upload the files, I'll run the
> script and show you the actual output.

**Nothing is wrong.** Not with your work, not with the repository, and not
with Claude. That answer is the prompt working exactly as written — the last
line asked Claude to say so plainly instead of inventing results, and it did.

Two things cause it, and they are worth telling apart.

**Web access may simply be switched off.** It is a setting, not a default. To
check: open **claude.ai**, click your name or initials in the lower-left
corner, choose **Settings**, and look for the web search or web access toggle.
If it is off, turn it on and start a *new* conversation — a conversation that
began without web access does not gain it partway through.

**Even with it on, a direct file link may not be fetchable.** Claude's web
tools follow links found on pages they have already loaded, and generally
refuse to open a URL constructed from scratch. That is why Path 2 points at a
plain page of links on the course site rather than at a code repository —
repositories serve their file listings through pages that block automated
fetching, and a filename printed as text is not a link anything can follow.

Either way, the fix is the same: use Path 1. It needs no settings, no search,
and no permission — and it is how most of this class will run the labs.

### The setting that actually matters

There is a second setting, and it matters far more than the first one.

Under **Settings → Capabilities**, find **Code execution and file creation**
and make sure it is **on**. On the Free, Pro, and Max plans you have to turn
this on yourself; it is not enabled by default.

::: {.scarlet}
Without it, Claude cannot run anything. It will read the script, understand it
perfectly well, and *describe* what the output would look like — in fluent,
confident prose, with numbers that came from nowhere.

That is not a broken lab. That is the exact failure this entire course is
organized against, arriving disguised as success.
:::

**How to tell the difference.** When code execution is on, you will see the
code actually run — a panel or block showing the script executing, and printed
output appearing beneath it. When it is off, you get prose. If Claude tells you
the series has 26,342 rows but you cannot find a line of output that *says*
26,342, the number is not evidence. Ask directly:

> Did you actually execute that script, or are you describing what it would
> produce? Show me the raw output.

An honest assistant will tell you. Then turn the setting on and start a new
conversation.

::: {.charcoal}
Do not let a stuck session turn into a fabricated answer. If Claude cannot get
the files, it should tell you — and if it ever reports numbers *without*
showing you the executed output that produced them, that is the failure this
whole course is organized against.
:::

### Where the data came from

You are analyzing a CSV, but somebody had to retrieve it. This is the code that
produced `data/dff.csv`, run once by your instructor rather than by each of you
thirty times:


```{python}
#| label: download-dff

from fred_tools import fred_series

dff = fred_series("DFF", start="2020-01-01").to_frame("federal_funds_rate")

missing_count = int(dff["federal_funds_rate"].isna().sum())

print(f"Downloaded {len(dff):,} DFF observations.")
print(f"Date range: {dff.index.min().date()} to {dff.index.max().date()}")
print(f"Missing rate values: {missing_count:,}")

dff.to_csv("dff_downloaded.csv")
print("Saved data to dff_downloaded.csv")
```

```{python}
#| label: dff-head
dff.head()
```

### Verification checklist

Do not stop when the program runs without an error. Verify that:

+ the file really is `DFF` — the Federal Funds Effective Rate — and not some
  neighbouring series with a similar name;
+ the index is stored as dates and the rate column is numeric;
+ the dates are **unique** and in order, before you trust any count or average
  computed from them;
+ FRED's `.` missing-value marker became a missing numeric value rather than
  the text `"."`;
+ the script reports rather than silently deletes missing observations;
+ the row count and latest date are plausible against the
  [FRED webpage for DFF](https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/DFF); and
+ every number in your write-up appears somewhere in the executed output above.

The third item is the one students skip. A duplicated date inflates every
count and can offset a genuine gap, so a coverage check that looks reassuring
may be measuring a broken series. Verify the thing you are measuring *with*,
not just the thing you are measuring.

::: {.scarlet}
A data request that succeeds establishes only that the server returned
something. It does not establish that we requested the correct concept, units,
frequency, dates, or transformation. Those are analytical responsibilities.
:::

Here is the check on data types, which is the one students skip most often:

```{python}
#| label: dff-dtypes
print(dff.dtypes)
print(f"\nIndex type: {type(dff.index).__name__}")
print(f"Any non-numeric values coerced to NaN: {missing_count}")
```

#| label: dff-decade-box

## Selecting versus calculating: an audit

The previous version of this note built a sequence of month-start dates and
used it to index the daily series directly. In R that looked like
`dff[my_months, ]`; the Python equivalent is a `.loc` lookup on a list of
dates. Both do the same thing, and it is worth being precise about what that
thing is.

```{python}
#| label: month-starts

my_months = pd.date_range("2020-01-01", pd.Timestamp.today().normalize(), freq="MS")
selected = dff.reindex(my_months)
selected.head(12)
```

::: {.scarlet}
This **selects particular daily observations** whose dates happen to be the
first of a month. It does **not calculate** a monthly federal funds rate.
:::

There is a second, quieter hazard in selecting by date. A requested date only
returns a value if the series actually has an observation on that day, and
whether it does depends on the series' publication calendar. Rather than assume,
we check:

```{python}
#| label: month-start-gaps

n_requested = len(my_months)
n_missing = int(selected["federal_funds_rate"].isna().sum())

print(f"Month-start dates requested: {n_requested}")
print(f"Dates with no observation:   {n_missing}")
if n_missing:
    print("Missing:", [d.date() for d in
                       selected.index[selected['federal_funds_rate'].isna()]][:12])
```

`DFF` is published on a 7-day daily calendar, so it has a value on weekends and
holidays and this lookup happens to find one every month. Run the same code
against a business-day series — `DGS10`, say, or `SP500` — and month-starts
that land on a weekend come back empty. Selecting by date is fragile in a way
that is invisible until the calendar changes underneath you.

### Three defensible alternatives

```{python}
#| label: monthly-alternatives

rate = dff["federal_funds_rate"]

monthly = pd.DataFrame({
    "mean":  rate.resample("MS").mean(),
    "first": rate.resample("MS").first(),
    "last":  rate.resample("MS").last(),
})
monthly.head(12).round(4)
```

Each answers a different business question:

+ the **monthly mean** describes average borrowing conditions *during* the
  month;
+ the **first available observation** describes the rate the month *opened*
  with; and
+ the **last available observation** describes the rate the month *closed*
  with.

These calculations produce different numbers. The correct transformation
depends on the question, and choosing one without stating the question is not a
technical shortcut — it is an unstated assumption.

```{python}
#| label: monthly-divergence

spread = (monthly["mean"] - monthly["last"]).abs()
print(f"Largest gap between the monthly mean and the month-end rate: "
      f"{spread.max():.3f} percentage points, in "
      f"{spread.idxmax().strftime('%B %Y')}.")
```

## Cross-sectional data

::: {.charcoal}
**Cross-sectional data** are values collected from a number of subjects (firms,
individuals, states, regions, etc.) during the same time period (or nearly the
same).
:::

State unemployment levels can also be retrieved from **FRED**. Conveniently,
the *symbol* for the unemployment rate for a state is the state's two letter
abbreviation followed by the letters "UR". The Nevada unemployment rate is
**NVUR**.

### Extending the workflow to cross-sectional data

The definition of a cross section requires more care than merely downloading 50
series. State unemployment observations are released on schedules that can
differ, and the latest non-missing date need not be identical for every state.
A defensible comparison must establish a common reference date or explicitly
document any timing differences.

The Laboratory 1 pack already contains this script and its data — you do not
need to download anything else. In the same conversation where you ran
`01a_inspect_dff.py`, ask Claude:

::: {.prompt}
Prompt

> Now run `01c_state_cross_section.py` from the files I uploaded. Before you
> compare any states, tell me whether every state's most recent observation
> falls on the same date. If the dates differ, report the differences and ask
> me to choose a common-date rule rather than silently combining unlike
> periods. Show me the actual output.
:::

::: {.charcoal}
This task introduces the habit the rest of the course depends on: **Claude
should surface a consequential analytical choice rather than quietly make it
for us.**

Notice that the prompt does not merely ask for the answer. It asks Claude to
*stop* at a specific point and hand a decision back. An assistant left to its
own devices will pick a rule — probably a reasonable one — and never mention
that a choice was made. The unstated assumption is the danger, not the rule
itself.
:::

```{python}
#| label: state-abbrevs

state_abb = [
    "AL", "AK", "AZ", "AR", "CA", "CO", "CT", "DE", "FL", "GA",
    "HI", "ID", "IL", "IN", "IA", "KS", "KY", "LA", "ME", "MD",
    "MA", "MI", "MN", "MS", "MO", "MT", "NE", "NV", "NH", "NJ",
    "NM", "NY", "NC", "ND", "OH", "OK", "OR", "PA", "RI", "SC",
    "SD", "TN", "TX", "UT", "VT", "VA", "WA", "WV", "WI", "WY",
]
print(f"{len(state_abb)} states")
```

R supplies `state.abb` as a built-in constant. Python does not, so we write the
list out. That is a small thing, but it is representative: several conveniences
that R bundles for statistical work have to be supplied explicitly in Python.

```{python}
#| label: state-download

rows = []
failures = []

for abb in state_abb:
    sid = f"{abb}UR"
    try:
        s = fred_series(sid, start="1976-01-01").dropna()
        rows.append({
            "State": abb,
            "Series": sid,
            "Date": s.index[-1],
            "UR": float(s.iloc[-1]),
        })
    except Exception as exc:
        failures.append({"State": abb, "Series": sid, "error": type(exc).__name__})

my_datfr = pd.DataFrame(rows)
print(f"Retrieved {len(my_datfr)} of {len(state_abb)} state series.")
if failures:
    print("Failures:", failures)
```

### Are these observations actually contemporaneous?

Before we treat this as a cross section, we check the assumption the term
depends on:

```{python}
#| label: date-alignment

date_counts = my_datfr["Date"].value_counts().sort_index()
print(date_counts.to_string())

if len(date_counts) == 1:
    print(f"\nAll {len(my_datfr)} states report the same date. "
          f"This is a clean cross section.")
else:
    print(f"\nWARNING: {len(date_counts)} distinct observation dates. "
          f"These states are NOT all measured in the same period.")
    common = date_counts.index.max()
    print(f"States not reporting on {common.date()}: "
          f"{sorted(my_datfr.loc[my_datfr['Date'] != common, 'State'])}")
```

If that check reports more than one date, we do not proceed by ignoring it. We
either restrict to a common date or we document the discrepancy in the write-up.

```{python}
#| label: state-table
my_datfr.sort_values("UR", ascending=False).reset_index(drop=True)
```

This is an example of a *cross-sectional* data set. We have the prevailing
state unemployment rate for
`{python} my_datfr['Date'].max().strftime('%A %B %d, %Y')` for all 50 US
States.

**Average US State Unemployment Rate**

The Census Bureau designates US States into defined regions and divisions.
Since the 1950s, this has included four statistical regions with 9
subdivisions. This list is available on
[Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_regions_of_the_United_States).

```{python}
#| label: state-regions

state_regions = {
    "new_england":        ["CT", "ME", "MA", "NH", "RI", "VT"],
    "mid_atlantic":       ["NJ", "NY", "PA"],
    "east_north_central": ["IL", "IN", "MI", "OH", "WI"],
    "west_north_central": ["IA", "KS", "MN", "MO", "NE", "ND", "SD"],
    "south_atlantic":     ["DE", "FL", "GA", "MD", "NC", "SC", "VA", "WV"],
    "east_south_central": ["AL", "KY", "MS", "TN"],
    "west_south_central": ["AR", "LA", "OK", "TX"],
    "mountain":           ["AZ", "CO", "ID", "MT", "NV", "NM", "UT", "WY"],
    "pacific":            ["AK", "CA", "HI", "OR", "WA"],
}

lookup = {
    st: (f"{i}. {name}", i)
    for i, (name, members) in enumerate(state_regions.items(), start=1)
    for st in members
}

my_datfr["Region"] = my_datfr["State"].map(lambda s: lookup[s][0])
my_datfr["Region_Index"] = my_datfr["State"].map(lambda s: lookup[s][1])

unassigned = my_datfr.loc[my_datfr["Region"].isna(), "State"].tolist()
print(f"States assigned to a region: {my_datfr['Region'].notna().sum()} "
      f"of {len(my_datfr)}")
if unassigned:
    print("Unassigned:", unassigned)
```

```{python}
#| label: region-box

regions = (my_datfr.sort_values("Region_Index")["Region"].drop_duplicates()
                    .tolist())
_ = box_plot([my_datfr.loc[my_datfr["Region"] == r, "UR"] for r in regions],
             labels=regions,
             title="State unemployment rates by Census region",
             xlab="Unemployment rate (percent)")
```

## Branches in statistics

::: {.scarlet}
The purpose of **descriptive statistics** is to summarize, or display, data to
quickly get an overview of the information.
:::

```{python}
#| label: descriptive-monthly
#| fig-cap: "Distribution of the month-start selections."

sel = selected["federal_funds_rate"].dropna()

fig_m, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 3.2))
ax.boxplot(sel.values, vert=False, widths=0.5,
           patch_artist=True,
           boxprops={"facecolor": UNLV_SCARLET, "alpha": 0.7},
           medianprops={"color": "white"})
ax.set_xlabel("Federal funds rate (percent)")
ax.set_yticks([])
ax.set_title("Month-start observations since 2020")
fig_m.tight_layout()
plt.show()

sel.describe().round(4)
```

```{python}
#| label: descriptive-full
#| fig-cap: "Distribution of the full daily series."

full = dff_full["DFF"].dropna()

fig_f, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 3.2))
ax.boxplot(full.values, vert=False, widths=0.5,
           patch_artist=True,
           boxprops={"facecolor": UNLV_SCARLET, "alpha": 0.7},
           medianprops={"color": "white"})
ax.set_xlabel("Federal funds rate (percent)")
ax.set_yticks([])
ax.set_title("Full daily history")
fig_f.tight_layout()
plt.show()

full.describe().round(4)
```

Descriptive statistics are useful, but have limitations. By summarizing large
quantities of data, you lose information. The two summaries above describe the
same underlying rate, and they disagree about nearly everything — because they
cover different periods. A summary statistic is only as meaningful as the
sample behind it.

```{python}
#| label: dff-timeseries

ts = dff_full.reset_index()
_ = time_series(ts["Date"], ts["DFF"],
                title="Federal Funds Effective Rate",
                ylab="Percent")
```

The time series plot shows structure — the 1980s peak, the long descent, the
zero lower bound, the recent tightening — that no box plot can express. This is
the information the summary discarded.

::: {.scarlet}
A **population** represents all possible subjects of interest. A **sample** is
a subset of a population.
:::

::: {.scarlet}
**Inferential statistics** allows us to make claims or conclusions about the
data and its population.
:::

Inferential statistics at work:

+ Production engineers tell us that a properly functioning production line will
  produce boxes of cereal with a weight of 18.0 oz.
+ We select a **random sample** of cereal from boxes coming from this
  production line (i.e., population).
+ We calculate the sample average to be 18.2 oz.
+ Using **inferential statistics**, we determine that the probability of
  observing a sample average of 18.2 oz is less than 1% if the actual
  population average were 18.0 oz.
+ Conclude that the actual population average is greater than 18.0 oz. That is,
  we find that there is a problem with this production line that needs to be
  solved.

::: {.scarlet}
**Predictive statistics** analyzes past data to predict future values and make
predictions.
:::

::: {.scarlet}
Data that describe a characteristic about a population are known as
**parameters**.
:::

::: {.scarlet}
Data that describe a characteristic about a sample are known as **statistics**.
:::

::: {.scarlet}
**Business analytics** uses statistical analysis and predictive models in the
business world to analyze data and make meaningful conclusions about decisions.
:::

::: {.scarlet}
**Data Analytics** uses statistical analysis and predictive models to answer
questions in the business world and more broadly to make meaningful conclusions
about decisions.
:::

## Ethics and statistics — it's a dangerous world of data out there

::: {.charcoal}
A **biased sample** is a sample that does not represent the intended population
and that can lead to distorted findings. Biased sampling can occur either
intentionally or unintentionally.
:::

One of the most frequent *abuses* of statistics that I notice regularly is the
focus on low probability events and the use of these outcomes in the
**headlines**. For example, a properly trained data analyst will report a 95%
confidence interval for a particular parameter. The analyst may say that there
is a 95% chance that the Nevada State net budget will range from
$(-\$750\text{ million}, \$2100\text{ million})$. It would be *misleading* in
an article to say that:

> Researchers find the State of Nevada is in budgetary peril: A budget
> shortfall of nearly \$1 Billion in the cards

When we see a wide ranging 95% confidence interval, the appropriate takeaway is
that there is a lot of **uncertainty** and a lot is **unknown** about the
processes. I believe journalists and politicians behave like they do because it
sells papers and can spur voting interest.

::: {.charcoal}
The same failure mode appears in AI-assisted work. An assistant will produce a
confident paragraph whether or not the underlying computation supports it.
Confidence in the prose is not evidence about the data. **Check the output.**
:::
